replacement: The result has been that the democratic revolution has taken place only in the material parts of society, without the accompanying change in laws, ideas, customs, and mores that was needed to make such a revolution beneficial. We have gotten a democracy, but without the conditions that would reduce its vices and bring out its natural advantages. And although we already see the evils it brings, we do not know the benefits it may offer.

While the power of the Crown, supported by the aristocracy, governed the nations of Europe in peace, society had, amid its misery, several advantages that are now hard to appreciate or even imagine. The power of one part of his subjects was an insurmountable barrier to the prince’s tyranny. The monarch felt that the multitude saw him as almost divine, and the respect he inspired gave him a reason to use his power justly. However high they stood above the people, the nobles could not help taking the calm and kindly interest in its fate that a shepherd takes in his flock. Without acknowledging the poor as their equals, they watched over the destiny of those whose welfare Providence had entrusted to their care. The people had never conceived of a social condition different from their own, and they did not expect ever to rank with their chiefs. They accepted benefits from their superiors without questioning their rights. They grew attached to them when they were merciful and just, and they submitted to their exactions without resistance or servility, as to the unavoidable visitations of the arm of God. Custom and the mores of the time had also created a kind of law amid the violence and set certain limits to oppression. The noble never suspected that anyone would try to deprive him of the privileges he believed to be legitimate, and the serf regarded his own inferiority as a consequence of the unchangeable order of nature. It is therefore easy to imagine that a mutual exchange of goodwill took place between two classes so differently endowed by fate. Inequality and misery existed in society then, but the souls of neither class were degraded. Men are not corrupted by exercising power or debased by the habit of obeying. They are corrupted by exercising a power they believe to be illegitimate, and by obeying a rule they consider usurped and oppressive. On one side were wealth, strength, and leisure, along with the refinements of luxury, the elegance of taste, the pleasures of wit, and the religion of art. On the other were labor and a crude ignorance. Yet among this coarse and ignorant multitude it was not uncommon to find energetic passions, generous feelings, deep religious convictions, and independent virtues. A body politic organized in this way could boast of its stability, its power, and above all its glory.

But the scene has now changed. Gradually the two ranks are mingling. The divisions that once separated mankind are being lowered, property is being divided, power is shared, the light of intelligence is spreading, and the abilities of all classes are being cultivated equally. The state becomes democratic, and the empire of democracy is slowly and peacefully introduced into the institutions and customs of the nation. I can imagine a society in which all men would profess an equal attachment and respect for the laws, of which they are the common authors. The authority of the state would be respected as necessary, though not as divine, and the subject’s loyalty to the chief magistrate would be not a passion but a calm and rational conviction. Every individual would possess rights he is sure to keep, and a kind of manly confidence and mutual courtesy would arise among all classes, equally far from pride and from baseness. The people, well aware of their true interests, would accept that to enjoy the advantages of society they must meet its demands. In such a state of things, the voluntary association of citizens could take the place of the individual efforts of the nobles, and the community would be protected equally from anarchy and from oppression.

There is one country in the world where the great revolution I am speaking of seems to have nearly reached its natural limits. It has been carried out there with ease and simplicity. Or rather, that country has arrived at the consequences of the democratic revolution we are going through without having experienced the revolution itself. The emigrants who settled on the shores of America at the beginning of the seventeenth century separated the democratic principle from all the principles that held it back in the old communities of Europe, and they transplanted it, unmixed, to the New World. There it has been allowed to grow in perfect freedom and to bring out its consequences in the laws by shaping the customs of the country.

It seems to me beyond doubt that sooner or later we will arrive, like the Americans, at an almost complete equality of conditions. But I do not conclude from this that we will necessarily be led to draw the same political consequences that the Americans have drawn from a similar social organization. I am far from supposing that they have chosen the only form of government a democracy can adopt. But the fact that the same underlying cause shapes laws and customs in both countries is enough to explain why we have such an immense interest in knowing its effects in each of them.

Whenever a point could be established from written documents, I went to the original text and to the most authentic and respected works. I have cited my authorities in the notes, and anyone may consult them. Whenever the question concerned an opinion, a political custom, or a remark about the customs of the country, I tried to consult the best-informed men I met. If the point was important or doubtful, I was not satisfied with one witness, but formed my opinion from the testimony of several. Here the reader must necessarily take my word. I could often have named people he knows, or who deserve to be known, as proof of what I say, but I have carefully avoided doing so. A stranger often hears important truths at his host’s fireside that the host would perhaps hide from the ear of a friend. The host consoles himself with his guest for the silence he is otherwise bound to keep, and the shortness of the traveler’s stay removes any fear that he will be indiscreet. I carefully noted down every conversation of this kind as soon as it happened, but these notes will never leave my writing case. I would rather weaken the force of my statements than add my name to the list of strangers who repay generous hospitality with later vexation and annoyance.

replacement: I could easily list a great number of secondary causes that have helped establish the democratic republic of the United States and that help maintain it. But among these favorable elements I discern two principal ones, which I hasten to point out. I have already observed that the origin of the American settlements can be seen as the first and most effective cause to which the present prosperity of the United States may be attributed. The Americans had the chances of birth in their favor. Their forefathers brought with them into the country that equality of conditions from which the democratic republic has very naturally grown. Nor was this all they did. Besides this republican state of society, the early settlers handed down to their descendants the customs, mores, and opinions that contribute most to the success of a republican form of government. When I reflect on the consequences of this first circumstance, I seem to see the destiny of America contained in the first Puritan who landed on those shores, just as the whole human race was represented by the first man.
